PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 86 — Lesson 110: Skin Cancer & Suspicious Lesion Management

FNP-level goal: Assess a changing or suspicious skin lesion in clinical context, recognize features that warrant timely biopsy or dermatology referral, distinguish preventive counseling from population screening claims, and communicate a safe follow-up plan across all skin tones.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate asymptomatic population screening from evaluation of a patient with a changing, bleeding, nonhealing, or otherwise suspicious lesion.
  • Use morphology, evolution, symptoms, patient risk factors, and full-skin context to identify concerning pigmented and nonpigmented lesions.
  • Apply the ABCDE and “ugly duckling” frameworks without treating them as substitutes for clinical judgment.
  • Recognize when urgent referral, biopsy by a trained clinician, pathology follow-up, or emergency care is appropriate.
  • Provide equitable sun-protection and self-awareness counseling without assuming risk from skin tone alone.

Part 1 — Screening and Diagnostic Evaluation Are Different

The USPSTF concludes that evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against routine clinician visual skin examination for skin-cancer screening in asymptomatic adolescents and adults. That I statement does not apply to a patient with a lesion that is changing in size, shape, color, or symptoms; a nonhealing sore; a bleeding papule; or an irregular mole. Those presentations require diagnostic evaluation and a plan, not a statement that “screening is not recommended.”

Ask why the patient is concerned and whether the lesion is new, evolving, bleeding, painful, itchy, nonhealing, or different from the person’s other lesions. Document exact site, size, morphology, color variation, border, surface, symptoms, duration, and change. Medical-quality clinical photographs, used with consent and according to privacy policy, may support comparison and referral but never replace an in-person exam or pathology when indicated.

Part 2 — Risk Assessment Is More Than Skin Tone

Risk factors can include personal or family history of melanoma or other skin cancer, prior severe sunburns, high cumulative UV exposure, tanning-bed use, many or atypical nevi, immunosuppression, genetic syndromes, and certain occupational/recreational exposures. Skin cancer occurs in all skin tones; darker skin can be associated with later diagnosis because lesions may be less recognized or access barriers may delay care. Examine the patient’s concern with the same seriousness regardless of complexion and remember acral, nail, mucosal, and less sun-exposed sites when symptoms or evolution suggest concern.

Part 3 — Melanoma Clues: ABCDE Plus Evolution

The ABCDE framework supports communication: Asymmetry, irregular Border, color Cvariation, increasing Diameter, and Evolving change. Melanomas may be smaller than the commonly taught 6-mm threshold, so evolution and the “ugly duckling” sign—a lesion that looks different from the patient’s other lesions—matter. New or changing pigmented lesions, changing nail pigmentation, or a symptomatic lesion should not be reassured solely because one ABCDE feature is absent.

Part 4 — Nonpigmented Lesions Matter Too

Basal and squamous cell carcinoma may present as a persistent pearly, translucent, scaly, crusted, ulcerated, tender, bleeding, or nonhealing lesion. A sore that heals and repeatedly returns, or a keratotic lesion that persists or changes, deserves reassessment. Differential diagnosis includes inflammatory disease, infection, trauma, benign keratoses, angiomas, warts, and other lesions. The FNP does not need to name every lesion perfectly to recognize when definitive dermatologic assessment or biopsy is needed.

Part 5 — Biopsy and Referral: Do Not Destroy the Diagnostic Pathway

Biopsy technique affects diagnosis and staging. If melanoma is suspected, coordinate a method that preserves the histopathologic information needed for diagnosis and management; do not casually shave, freeze, cauterize, or otherwise destroy a suspicious lesion without considering whether tissue diagnosis is required and whether you have the appropriate training and pathway. Urgent dermatology referral is reasonable for a rapidly changing or highly suspicious lesion, new concerning nail pigmentation, possible melanoma, lesion in an anatomically complex site, diagnostic uncertainty, immunosuppressed patients, or a lesion that cannot be safely or confidently managed in primary care.

Closed-loop care is mandatory: record the referral/biopsy plan, pathology result, patient notification, definitive-treatment plan, and surveillance responsibility. A pathology report in an inbox without documented patient follow-up is an unsafe unfinished task.

Part 6 — Prevention and Counseling

Recommend practical UV protection: shade when feasible, protective clothing/hat/sunglasses, broad-spectrum sunscreen used as directed, and avoidance of indoor tanning. Counseling should fit the patient’s work, culture, cost, sensory tolerance, and climate. Encourage skin awareness: notice changing/nonhealing/bleeding lesions and seek assessment promptly. Avoid alarming patients with a false promise that sunscreen alone eliminates skin-cancer risk.

Part 7 — Urgency and Safety

Emergency evaluation is appropriate for a lesion with uncontrolled bleeding, a rapidly spreading painful infection, severe allergic reaction/anaphylaxis, or another acute systemic problem. Most suspicious lesions need timely—not emergency-department—dermatology/biopsy coordination. The key FNP decision is to choose the correct urgency, preserve diagnostic tissue, and ensure follow-up actually occurs.

Clinical Case

A 51-year-old with no prior skin-cancer history reports a dark spot on the sole that has enlarged and developed uneven color over six months. It looks different from all other moles. The patient has dark skin and was previously told not to worry about melanoma.

FNP reasoning: melanoma can occur in all skin tones and may arise on acral sites. Evolution, color variation, and ugly-duckling difference warrant timely diagnostic referral/biopsy planning. Do not dismiss the lesion based on skin tone or the absence of extensive sun exposure.

FNP Suspicious Lesion Framework

  1. Clarify the task: screening discussion versus diagnostic evaluation of a changing/symptomatic lesion.
  2. Describe and document: site, morphology, size, color, border, surface, symptoms, evolution, and risk factors.
  3. Use pattern recognition: ABCDE, ugly duckling, nonhealing/bleeding features, and patient-specific context.
  4. Choose the safe pathway: trained biopsy or timely dermatology referral; do not destroy tissue when melanoma is possible.
  5. Close the loop: pathology/referral result, patient communication, treatment/surveillance plan, prevention and return precautions.

High-Yield Summary

USPSTF I statement: concerns routine screening in asymptomatic people; it does not apply to a changing or suspicious lesion.
Melanoma clues: ABCDE, evolution, and ugly-duckling difference; small lesions can still be concerning.
Nonpigmented cancer clues: persistent, bleeding, crusted, tender, ulcerated, or nonhealing lesions.
Equity: skin cancer can occur in every skin tone; do not dismiss acral/nail/mucosal or evolving lesions.
FNP standard: preserve the diagnostic pathway and own pathology/referral follow-up.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Skin-lesion examination, photography, biopsy, pathology interpretation, dermatology referral, cancer surveillance, and emergency disposition must follow current guidelines, local policy, collaboration/scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
